Main article: [Architecture of Malta](/wiki/Architecture_of_Malta "Architecture of Malta")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Valletta_Lower_Barrakka_gardens_Malta_2014_2.jpg/250px-Valletta_Lower_Barrakka_gardens_Malta_2014_2.jpg)](/wiki/File:Valletta_Lower_Barrakka_gardens_Malta_2014_2.jpg)

[Lower Barrakka Gardens](/wiki/Lower_Barrakka_Gardens "Lower Barrakka Gardens")

Maltese architecture has been influenced by many different Mediterranean cultures and British architecture over its history.[[309]](#cite_note-311) The first settlers on the island constructed [Ġgantija](/wiki/%C4%A0gantija "Ġgantija"), one of the oldest manmade freestanding structures in the world. The Neolithic temple builders (3800–2500 BC) endowed the numerous temples of Malta and Gozo with intricate bas-relief designs.

The Roman period introduced highly decorative mosaic floors, marble colonnades, and classical statuary, remnants of which are beautifully preserved and presented in the Roman Domus, a country villa just outside the walls of [Mdina](/wiki/Mdina "Mdina"). The early Christian frescoes that decorate the [catacombs](/wiki/Catacombs "Catacombs") beneath Malta reveal a propensity for eastern, [Byzantine](/wiki/Byzantine "Byzantine") tastes. These tastes continued to inform the endeavours of [medieval](/wiki/Medieval "Medieval") Maltese artists, but they were increasingly influenced by the [Romanesque](/wiki/Romanesque_art "Romanesque art") and [Southern French Gothic](/wiki/Southern_French_Gothic "Southern French Gothic") movements.

Women in the United States Senate :: part 05 :: chunk_0004
Patty Murray holds the record as the longest serving woman senator. As a serving senator, her record is continuously extended.

In 2012, a record five new female senators were elected. This beat the record of four new female senators from 1992 and set the record of five new women and eleven female senators in one Senate class. The five new women were Democrats [Tammy Baldwin](/wiki/Tammy_Baldwin "Tammy Baldwin") of [Wisconsin](/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Wisconsin "List of United States senators from Wisconsin"), [Heidi Heitkamp](/wiki/Heidi_Heitkamp "Heidi Heitkamp") of [North Dakota](/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_North_Dakota "List of United States senators from North Dakota"), [Mazie Hirono](/wiki/Mazie_Hirono "Mazie Hirono") of [Hawaii](/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Hawaii "List of United States senators from Hawaii"), [Elizabeth Warren](/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren "Elizabeth Warren") of [Massachusetts](/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Massachusetts "List of United States senators from Massachusetts"), and Republican [Deb Fischer](/wiki/Deb_Fischer "Deb Fischer") of [Nebraska](/wiki/List_of_United_States_senators_from_Nebraska "List of United States senators from Nebraska"). Hirono was the first Asian-American woman and first Buddhist in the Senate, and Baldwin was the first openly gay person in the Senate.

In 2014, [Joni Ernst](/wiki/Joni_Ernst "Joni Ernst") was elected as the first female combat veteran to serve in the Senate. In 2016, [Catherine Cortez Masto](/wiki/Catherine_Cortez_Masto "Catherine Cortez Masto") was elected as the first Latina senator, while [Tammy Duckworth](/wiki/Tammy_Duckworth "Tammy Duckworth") was elected as the first female double amputee in the Senate.[[12]](#cite_note-14) In a June 2016 primary election, as a result of California's recent establishment of the [top-two primary](/wiki/Top-two_primary "Top-two primary"), [Attorney Gene

In 1793, [Lucinda Foote](/wiki/Lucinda_Foote "Lucinda Foote") passed the entrance exams for Yale College, but was rejected by the president on the basis of her gender.[[45]](#cite_note-bookof-46) Women studied at Yale from 1892, in graduate-level programs at the [Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences](/wiki/Yale_Graduate_School_of_Arts_and_Sciences "Yale Graduate School of Arts and Sciences").[[46]](#cite_note-47) The first seven women to earn PhDs received their degrees in 1894: [Elizabeth Deering Hanscom](/wiki/Elizabeth_Deering_Hanscom "Elizabeth Deering Hanscom"), Cornelia H. B. Rogers, Sara Bulkley Rogers, [Margaretta Palmer](/wiki/Margaretta_Palmer "Margaretta Palmer"), [Mary Augusta Scott](/wiki/Mary_Augusta_Scott "Mary Augusta Scott"), Laura Johnson Wylie, and [Charlotte Fitch Roberts](/wiki/Charlotte_Fitch_Roberts "Charlotte Fitch Roberts"). There is a portrait of them in [Sterling Memorial Library](/wiki/Sterling_Memorial_Library "Sterling Memorial Library"), painted by [Brenda Zlamany](/wiki/Brenda_Zlamany "Brenda Zlamany").[[47]](#cite_note-48)

In 1966, Yale began discussions with its [sister school](/wiki/Sister_school "Sister school") [Vassar College](/wiki/Vassar_College "Vassar College") about merging to foster coeducation at the undergraduate level. Vassar, then all-female and part of the [Seven Sisters](/wiki/Seven_Sisters_(colleges) "Seven Sisters (colleges)")—elite higher education schools that served as sister institutions to the [Ivy League](/wiki/Ivy_League "Ivy League") when nearly all Ivy League institutions still only admitted men—tentatively accepted, but then declined the invitation. **Rio de Janeiro**,[[a]](#cite_note-8) also known simply as **Rio**,[[8]](#cite_note-9) is the capital of the [state of Rio de Janeiro](/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro_(state) "Rio de Janeiro (state)"). It is the [second-most-populous city](/wiki/List_of_cities_in_Brazil_by_population "List of cities in Brazil by population") in [Brazil](/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") after [São Paulo](/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo "São Paulo") and the [sixth-most-populous city](/wiki/Largest_cities_in_the_Americas "Largest cities in the Americas") in the [Americas](/wiki/Americas "Americas").

Founded in 1565, the city was initially the seat of the [Captaincy of Rio de Janeiro](/wiki/Captaincy_of_Rio_de_Janeiro "Captaincy of Rio de Janeiro"), a domain of the [Portuguese Empire](/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire"). In 1763, it became the capital of the [State of Brazil](/wiki/State_of_Brazil "State of Brazil"). In 1808, when the [Portuguese Royal Court moved to Brazil](/wiki/Transfer_of_the_Portuguese_Court_to_Brazil "Transfer of the Portuguese Court to Brazil"), Rio de Janeiro became the seat of the court of Queen [Maria I of Portugal](/wiki/Maria_I_of_Portugal "Maria I of Portugal"). Under the leadership of her son, prince regent [John of Braganza](/wiki/John_VI_of_Portugal "John VI of Portugal"), Maria raised Brazil to the dignity of a kingdom within the [United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil, and Algarves](/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Portugal,_Brazil_and_the_Algarves "United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves"). Rio remained as the capital of the [pluricontinental](/wiki/Pluricontinentalism "Pluricontinentalism") monarchy until 1822, when the [Brazilian War of Independence](/wiki/Brazilian_War_of_Independence "Brazilian War of Independence") began. This is one of the few instances in history that the capital of a colonizing country officially shifted to a city in one of its colonies. In 1997, Destiny's Child performed as an opening act on SWV and [the O'Jays](/wiki/The_O%27Jays "The O'Jays")' respective concert tours, in order to promote *Destiny's Child*.[[13]](#cite_note-soetan-13) "No, No, No" was subsequently released as their debut single, and the [lead single](/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single") from *Destiny's Child*, on October 27.[[29]](#cite_note-31) The song's two versions were strategically given a dual release, to ensure chart success.[[13]](#cite_note-soetan-13) "No, No, No" eventually reached its peak at number three on the US [*Billboard* Hot 100](/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"),[[30]](#cite_note-32) and became the ninth best-selling single of 1998 in the US.[[31]](#cite_note-33) *Destiny's Child* was released on February 17, 1998.[[22]](#cite_note-o'brien-23) It was initially promoted with an appearance at the [1998 Soul Train Music Awards](/wiki/1998_Soul_Train_Music_Awards "1998 Soul Train Music Awards") on February 27,[[22]](#cite_note-o'brien-23) and a performance on *[Live with Regis and Kathie Lee](/wiki/Live_with_Kelly_and_Mark "Live with Kelly and Mark")* on April 20; the latter was their debut televised performance.[[32]](#cite_note-34) The album debuted at number 69 on the US [*Billboard* 200](/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") chart dated March 7, 1998,[[33]](#cite_note-35) peaking at number 67 four weeks later.[[34]](#cite_note-36) Meanwhile, it debuted and peaked at number 14 on the US [Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums](/wiki/Top_R%26B/Hip-Hop_Albums "Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums").[[35]](#cite_note-BBR&B-37) In the UK, where the album debuted and peaked at number 45 on the [UK Albums Chart](/wiki/UK_Albums_Chart "UK Albums Chart"),[[36]](#cite_note-occ-38) Destiny's Child performed "No, No, No" on the *[Top of the Pops](/wiki/Top_of_the_Pops "Top of the Pops")* episode dated March 27, 1998,[[37]](#cite_note-39) and "With Me" on the episode dated July 10.[[38]

In 1975 he moved to a professor position at [Paris VI University](/wiki/Paris_VI_University "Paris VI University"). At the same time he taught in other institutions, in particular at the [École polytechnique](/wiki/%C3%89cole_polytechnique "École polytechnique") (1973–1984), [MIT](/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (1980), [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") (1981), [Yale University](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") (1984–1993) and [Conservatoire national des arts et métiers](/wiki/Conservatoire_national_des_arts_et_m%C3%A9tiers "Conservatoire national des arts et métiers") (2000). He was head of the Physics department at the [École normale supérieure](/wiki/%C3%89cole_Normale_Sup%C3%A9rieure "École Normale Supérieure") from 1994 to 2000.

Since 2001, Haroche has been a professor at the Collège de France and holds the [chair of quantum physics](/wiki/Quantum_mechanics "Quantum mechanics"). Main articles: [James Earl Jones on screen and stage](/wiki/James_Earl_Jones_on_screen_and_stage "James Earl Jones on screen and stage") and [List of awards and nominations received by James Earl Jones](/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_James_Earl_Jones "List of awards and nominations received by James Earl Jones")

Jones had an extensive career in film, television, and theater. He started out in film by appearing in the 1964 political satire film *[Dr. Strangelove](/wiki/Dr._Strangelove "Dr. Strangelove")* as Lt. Lothar Zogg. He then went on to star in the 1970 film *[The Great White Hope](/wiki/The_Great_White_Hope_(film) "The Great White Hope (film)")* as Jack Jefferson, a role he first played at Washington's Arena Stage in the world premier of Howard Sackler's play of the [same name](/wiki/The_Great_White_Hope "The Great White Hope").[[133]](#cite_note-Marks2024-133)

On television, he received two [Primetime Emmy Awards](/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award "Primetime Emmy Award") for his roles in thriller film *[Heat Wave](/wiki/Heat_Wave_(1990_film) "Heat Wave (1990 film)")* (1990) and the crime series *[Gabriel's Fire](/wiki/Gabriel%27s_Fire "Gabriel's Fire")* (1991). He also acted in *[Jesus of Nazareth](/wiki/Jesus_of_Nazareth_(TV_series) "Jesus of Nazareth (TV series)")* (1977), *[Roots: The Next Generations](/wiki/Roots:_The_Next_Generations "Roots: The Next Generations")* (1979) and *[Picket Fences](/wiki/Picket_Fences "Picket Fences")* (1994), and *[Homicide: Life on the Street](/wiki/Homicide:_Life_on_the_Street "Homicide: Life on the Street")* (1997). Through the Paris 2024 Games, French athletes had won 815 medals at the [Summer Olympic Games](/wiki/Summer_Olympic_Games "Summer Olympic Games") in a wide variety of sports, achieving particular success in [fencing](/wiki/Fencing "Fencing"), [cycling](/wiki/Cycle_sport "Cycle sport") and [judo](/wiki/Judo "Judo"). France has won an additional 138 medals at the [Winter Olympic Games](/wiki/Winter_Olympic_Games "Winter Olympic Games"), notably in [alpine skiing](/wiki/Alpine_skiing "Alpine skiing") and [biathlon](/wiki/Biathlon "Biathlon").

Several French athletes have left a significant mark on Olympic history. Biathlete [Martin Fourcade](/wiki/Martin_Fourcade "Martin Fourcade") holds the national record for Olympic titles with six gold medals, followed by judoka [Teddy Riner](/wiki/Teddy_Riner "Teddy Riner") and fellow biathlete [Quentin Fillon Maillet](/wiki/Quentin_Fillon_Maillet "Quentin Fillon Maillet"), each with five gold medals. The record for the most total Olympic medals by a French athlete is held by Fillon Maillet, who won nine medals overall between 2022 and 2026. Fillon Maillet is followed by fencers [Philippe Cattiau](/wiki/Philippe_Cattiau "Philippe Cattiau") and [Roger Ducret](/wiki/Roger_Ducret "Roger Ducret"), each with eight medals earned during the 1920s and 1930s. Fourcade and Riner follow closely with seven medals each, and are trailed by fellow fencing legends [Lucien Gaudin](/wiki/Lucien_Gaudin "Lucien Gaudin"), [Christian d'Oriola](/wiki/Christian_d%27Oriola "Christian d'Oriola"), and [Philippe Riboud](/wiki/Philippe_Riboud "Philippe Riboud"), who each amassed six medals over their Olympic careers.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Fm_shiba_inu_puppy.jpg/250px-Fm_shiba_inu_puppy.jpg)](/wiki/File:Fm_shiba_inu_puppy.jpg)

A Shiba Inu puppy

The Shiba Inu is considered an alert, affectionate, and independent breed with high intelligence but also somewhat stubborn and strong-willed.[[11]](#cite_note-Spruce-11)

The terms "spirited boldness" (悍威, *kan'i*), "good nature" (良性, *ryōsei*), and "artlessness" (素朴, *soboku*) have subtle interpretations that have been the subject of much commentary.[[12]](#cite_note-detailedstudy-12)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Shiba_inu_puppy_and_adult.jpg/250px-Shiba_inu_puppy_and_adult.jpg)](/wiki/File:Shiba_inu_puppy_and_adult.jpg)

A Shiba Inu puppy and an adult

A survey of experts classified the Shiba Inu as having "high aggression, high reactivity and medium trainability".[[13]](#cite_note-TAKEUCHI_MORI_2006_pp._789–796-13) A possible explanation for this and other observed behaviour is that the Shiba Inu is more closely related to the [wolf](/wiki/Wolf "Wolf") than domesticated dogs from other countries.[[14]](#cite_note-Parker_Kim_Sutter_Carlson_2004_pp._1160–1164-14) Due to the high intelligence of the breed it requires a lot of exercise and stimulation. Insufficient exercise may lead to anxiety which leads to undesirable behaviours, notably the "shiba scream".[[11]](#cite_note-Spruce-11)[[9]](#cite_note-PetMD-9) The Shiba Inu has a reputation for being "aloof" and early socialization as a puppy is key for the dog to get along with other people and animals.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

A survey in Japan found the Shiba Inu to be more likely to engage in destructive behaviour, refusal to walk whilst on a lead, engage in [mounting](/wiki/Copulation_(zoology) "Copulation (zoology)") behaviour, and tail chasing. The Shiba Inu was also found to be less likely to bark at noises whilst inside the house.[[16]](#cite_note-16)

During the week of September 25, 2005, Carey set another record, becoming the first female to occupy the first two spots atop the Hot 100, as "We Belong Together" remained at number one, and her next single, "[Shake It Off](/wiki/Shake_It_Off_(Mariah_Carey_song) "Shake It Off (Mariah Carey song)")", held the number two spot.[[29]](#cite_note-records-29) Additionally, the song held the top position on the official [Hot 100 Airplay](/wiki/Hot_100_Airplay_(Radio_Songs) "Hot 100 Airplay (Radio Songs)") chart for sixteen weeks, tying for the second all time spot with [No Doubt](/wiki/No_Doubt "No Doubt")'s "[Don't Speak](/wiki/Don%27t_Speak "Don't Speak")" (1996).[[29]](#cite_note-records-29) "We Belong Together" was certified [6× Platinum](/wiki/RIAA_certifications "RIAA certifications") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA), denoting shipments of 6 million copies throughout the United States.[[34]](#cite_note-riaa-34) On the [*Billboard* Hot 100 Year-end Chart](/wiki/Billboard_Year-End "Billboard Year-End") of 2005, the song was declared the number one song, a career first for Carey.[[35]](#cite_note-US_yearend-35) *Billboard* listed "We Belong Together" ninth on the Billboard Hot 100 All-Time Top Songs[[36]](#cite_note-yahoosales-36) and second on Top Billboard Hot 100 R&B/Hip-Hop Songs.[[37]](#cite_note-yahoosales2-37) On the Hot 100, "We Belong Together" spent twenty-three consecutive weeks in the Top 10 and forty-three weeks total on the chart, making it Carey's longest running Top 10 song and her longest charting hit at the time.
